content: 1. There is no available data on mortality, hospital admissions, or other clinically relevant outcomes related to the use of umifenovir. The results presented are based on indirect comparisons. 2. The studies did not include patients with zoonotic influenza, and the specific types of influenza virus infections were not reported. 3. Characteristics of the studies, risk of bias ratings, and effect estimates for outcomes related to umifenovir use have been previously published. 4. For patients with non-severe influenza, the GRADE Summary of Findings outlines the relative and absolute effects of umifenovir compared to placebo or standard care for outcomes of interest, along with certainty ratings informed by network meta-analyses (NMA). 5. Recommendations for patients with non-severe symptomatic influenza (suspected or confirmed) include subgroup analyses requested by the guideline development group (GDG). These analyses focused on influenza type (seasonal, zoonotic, pandemic), confirmed versus suspected infection, age groups (children under 2 years, children versus adults, adolescents versus older adults aged ≥65 years), and patients at increased risk of poor outcomes versus those not at risk. However, sufficient data were unavailable to inform these subgroup analyses. 6. Umifenovir has little to no effect on mortality, with a difference of 0.3 fewer deaths per 1,000 patients (95% CI: 0.7 fewer to 0.72 more). 7. Umifenovir has little to no effect on hospital admissions, with a difference of 15 fewer admissions per 1,000 patients (95% CI: 21 fewer to 120 more). However, the certainty of this evidence is very low due to serious risk of bias and imprecision. 8. There is no randomized controlled trial (RCT) data available to determine whether umifenovir increases the emergence of antiviral resistance. 9. It is very uncertain whether umifenovir increases adverse events related to treatment, with a difference of 52 fewer adverse events per 1,000 patients (95% CI: 94 fewer to 45 more). 10. There is no RCT data available to assess whether umifenovir increases serious adverse events. 11. Umifenovir may reduce the time to alleviation of symptoms, but the evidence is of low certainty due to serious risk of bias and imprecision. 12. The risk of bias in the studies was serious, primarily due to inadequate concealment of allocation during randomization, leading to potential selection bias. Imprecision was also a concern due to wide confidence intervals. 13. Zanamivir is strongly recommended against for patients with suspected or confirmed non-severe influenza virus infection, based on moderate-quality evidence. 14. Zanamivir treatment may have no significant effect on the time to alleviation of symptoms, mortality, or hospital admissions due to the low absolute risk of severe influenza. 15. Zanamivir may have little to no effect on adverse events, serious adverse events, or the emergence of resistance. 16. In clinical trials, zanamivir was administered within 2 days of symptom onset in patients with non-severe influenza virus infection. 17. The certainty of evidence for zanamivir was rated as high for mortality and hospital admission, moderate for time to alleviation of symptoms, and low for adverse events, serious adverse events, and emergence of resistance. 18. Almost all well-informed patients with non-severe influenza virus infection would likely choose not to use zanamivir. 19. Zanamivir is an inhaled powdered medication requiring an inhaler device, which may not be suitable for young children or older adults who may struggle to properly inhale the medication. 20. Patients with chronic pulmonary disease should avoid inhaled zanamivir due to the increased risk of bronchospasm. 21. Zanamivir may not be available in some countries. 22. The GDG inferred that the threshold for zanamivir use in non-severe influenza would be a reduction in symptom alleviation time by at least 1 day. However, evidence suggests no important benefit in hospitalization, mortality, or symptom improvement. 23. The evidence regarding zanamivir versus placebo or standard care was informed by 19 RCTs enrolling 7,735 patients with non-severe illnesses. Most studies enrolled less than 20% of patients with comorbidities or did not report comorbidity details. 24. None of the included studies enrolled infants under 5 years of age or pregnant individuals. 25. Subgroup analyses for zanamivir versus placebo or standard care did not reveal any subgroup effects for influenza type, confirmed versus suspected infection, or risk of adverse events. 26. Antibiotics are strongly recommended against for patients with suspected or confirmed non-severe influenza virus infection and a low probability of bacterial co-infection, based on low-quality evidence. 27. The systematic review found very limited evidence regarding the impact of antibiotic administration on outcomes for patients with non-severe influenza and low probability of bacterial infection. 28. It is very uncertain whether antibiotics have any impact on disease progression in patients with non-severe influenza and low probability of bacterial infection. 29. The evidence suggests that antibiotics have little to no effect on mortality in this population due to the low baseline risk of death. 30. Adverse event data from antibiotics were limited due to small patient numbers in available direct evidence. However, indirect evidence from observational studies highlights the adverse effects of widespread antibiotic use. 31. The GDG emphasized the risk of antimicrobial resistance from widespread antibiotic use in a disease as prevalent as influenza, which could limit future treatment options for bacterial respiratory tract infections. 32. The certainty of evidence for concomitant antibiotic use in non-severe influenza was very low, with only a small number of RCTs informing the evidence. 33. The GDG inferred that almost all well-informed patients with non-severe influenza and low risk of bacterial infection would choose not to take concomitant antibiotics. 34. The GDG strongly preferred avoiding antibiotics in patients with a low probability of concurrent bacterial infection to preserve the effectiveness of antibiotics for treatable bacterial infections. 35. The evidence regarding concomitant use of antibiotics versus no antibiotics was informed by four RCTs enrolling 331 non-hospitalized patients with confirmed symptomatic influenza. 36. Indirect evidence provides moderate certainty of an increase in adverse effects with antibiotic use. 37. The panel placed high importance on the likelihood of resistance emergence with widespread antibiotic use in a condition as common as influenza. 38. For all other outcomes, the certainty of evidence was low. 39. The WHO generally avoids strong recommendations when evidence for critical outcomes is of low certainty. However, in cases where low-quality evidence suggests benefit and moderateor high-quality evidence of harm exists, strong recommendations may be appropriate. 40. Given the significant risk of adverse events with antibiotics and no evidence of benefit in outcomes of interest, the GDG judged that most patients would not choose to use antibiotics in the setting of non-severe influenza with a low probability of bacterial infection.
